subject: Renal
vignette: A 14-year-old boy has microscopic hematuria since childhood and gradually progressive hearing loss. Ophthalmologic examination reveals anterior lenticonus and retinopathy. His maternal uncle required dialysis in his 30s. The physician recognizes a classic inherited syndrome.
question: Which of the following best summarizes the classic clinical triad of this syndrome?

options.text: Hematuria, hypertension, and edema
Eye problems (eg, anterior lenticonus, retinopathy), glomerulonephritis, and sensorineural hearing loss
Hearing loss, hypocalcemia, and renal tubular acidosis
Cataracts, diabetes insipidus, and nephrolithiasis
Retinitis pigmentosa, ataxia, and polyneuropathy

explanation_correct: Alport syndrome is classically remembered as the inability to see, pee, or hear a bee: eye abnormalities including anterior lenticonus and retinopathy, glomerulonephritis with hematuria progressing to renal failure, and sensorineural hearing loss. The positive family history and the combination of ocular, renal, and auditory findings in this boy are characteristic. Anterior lenticonus is a particularly specific ocular marker.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hematuria with hypertension and edema describes a nephritic syndrome but lacks the characteristic ocular and auditory involvement of Alport syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hearing loss with hypocalcemia and renal tubular acidosis is not the Alport triad; hearing loss in Alport is sensorineural without those tubular abnormalities.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cataracts, diabetes insipidus, and nephrolithiasis are not features of Alport syndrome and do not form a recognized inherited triad here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Retinitis pigmentosa with ataxia and polyneuropathy suggests a mitochondrial or neurologic disorder, not the type IV collagen defect of Alport syndrome.

educationalObjective: Alport syndrome presents with ocular disease, glomerulonephritis, and sensorineural hearing loss.

subject: Renal
vignette: A geneticist counsels a family with Alport syndrome. The disease appears in multiple generations, affects males more severely, and the affected father's daughters are carriers who may have mild hematuria. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in a collagen gene.
question: Which of the following best describes the underlying genetic defect and inheritance of Alport syndrome?

options.text: Mutation in type I collagen with autosomal recessive inheritance
Mutation in type III collagen with autosomal dominant inheritance
Mutation in type IV collagen with mitochondrial inheritance
Mutation in type IV collagen altering the GBM, mostly X-linked dominant
Mutation in laminin with X-linked recessive inheritance

explanation_correct: Alport syndrome results from mutations in type IV collagen, a structural component of the glomerular basement membrane, cochlea, and lens. The alteration of the GBM produces the renal disease. It is mostly X-linked dominant, which explains the more severe course in males and the milder hematuria that can appear in carrier females.

explanation_incorrect.A: Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta, not Alport syndrome, and Alport is not autosomal recessive in its classic form.
explanation_incorrect.B: Type III collagen mutations are associated with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, not Alport syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.C: Although type IV collagen is correct, Alport syndrome is not mitochondrially inherited; mitochondrial hearing loss disorders are distinct.
explanation_incorrect.E: The defective protein is type IV collagen, not laminin, and the classic inheritance is X-linked dominant rather than X-linked recessive.

educationalObjective: Alport syndrome is caused by type IV collagen mutations that alter the GBM and is mostly X-linked dominant.

subject: Renal
vignette: A kidney biopsy from a 16-year-old boy with hereditary nephritis and hearing loss is examined by electron microscopy. The glomerular basement membrane shows irregular areas of thinning and thickening with longitudinal splitting, creating a pattern the pathologist describes as 'basket-weave.'
question: Which of the following is the hallmark ultrastructural finding of Alport syndrome?

options.text: Irregular thinning and thickening with splitting of the GBM producing a 'basket-weave' appearance
Subepithelial electron-dense humps
Diffuse thickening of the GBM with subepithelial deposits
Electron-dense intramembranous deposits (dense deposit disease)
Effacement of podocyte foot processes with no GBM abnormality

explanation_correct: The characteristic ultrastructural lesion of Alport syndrome is irregular thinning and thickening of the GBM with longitudinal splitting, producing the classic basket-weave appearance on electron microscopy. This reflects the defective type IV collagen network. It corresponds to the light-microscopic finding of irregular GBM changes and underlies the progressive hematuria and renal failure.

explanation_incorrect.B: Subepithelial electron-dense humps are the hallmark of infection-related, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, not Alport syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.C: Diffuse GBM thickening with subepithelial deposits describes membranous nephropathy, not the irregular basket-weave splitting of Alport.
explanation_incorrect.D: Intramembranous dense deposits define MPGN type II, also called dense deposit disease, a different entity.
explanation_incorrect.E: Isolated foot-process effacement with a normal GBM is the lesion of minimal change disease, not a collagen IV disorder.

educationalObjective: Alport syndrome shows irregular GBM thinning and thickening with longitudinal splitting giving a basket-weave appearance on EM.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 12-year-old boy with hematuria and sensorineural hearing loss undergoes renal biopsy. Immunofluorescence is negative for IgG, IgM, and C3, and the pathologist notes that staining is generally nonspecific and usually remains negative. Electron microscopy confirms irregular GBM splitting.
question: Which of the following best explains the immunofluorescence findings in Alport syndrome?

options.text: Linear IgG deposition along the GBM, as in anti-GBM disease
Granular subendothelial IgG and C3 deposition, as in lupus nephritis
Negative or nonspecific immunofluorescence because the defect is a structural collagen IV protein, not immune-complex deposition
Dominant mesangial IgA deposition, as in Berger disease
Pauci-immune staining with PR3-ANCA positivity

explanation_correct: Alport syndrome is a structural disease of type IV collagen, not an immune-mediated glomerulonephritis, so immunofluorescence is initially negative or shows only nonspecific staining and usually stays negative. The diagnosis rests on the clinical triad, family history, and the characteristic basket-weave GBM on electron microscopy. This contrasts with immune-complex diseases that show granular Ig and complement deposition and with anti-GBM disease that shows linear IgG.

explanation_incorrect.A: Linear IgG deposition indicates anti-GBM, or Goodpasture, disease, an antibody-mediated process not present in Alport syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.B: Granular subendothelial IgG and C3 are features of diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis, not a structural collagen disorder.
explanation_incorrect.D: Mesangial IgA deposition defines IgA nephropathy, which is immune-complex mediated, unlike Alport syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pauci-immune staining with PR3-ANCA is characteristic of ANCA-associated vasculitis such as GPA, not Alport syndrome.

educationalObjective: Alport syndrome has negative or nonspecific immunofluorescence because it is a structural type IV collagen defect, not an immune-complex disease.
